content: H7N3 is a subtype of the Influenza A virus, which is sometimes referred to as the bird flu virus. In February 2004, the presence of H7N3 was confirmed at several poultry farms in British Columbia, Canada. By April 2004, 18 farms in the region had been quarantined to prevent further spread of the virus. Two human cases of H7N3 infection were confirmed in the area, with symptoms including conjunctivitis and mild influenza-like illness. Both individuals fully recovered. The H7N3 strain was first identified in turkeys in Britain in 1963. According to the World Health Organization (WHO) and the World Organisation for Animal Health, one of its last known appearances in poultry occurred in Canada in April and May 2004. In 2004, an outbreak of the less virulent H5N2 strain of bird flu in Taiwan led to the culling of hundreds of thousands of birds. Additionally, in November 2005, Taiwan detected a highly pathogenic strain of H7N3 in droppings left by a migratory bird. Authorities conducted tests to determine whether the virus had spread to nearby poultry farms. In April 2006, H7N3 was detected in the United Kingdom for the first time since 1979. The virus infected birds and one poultry worker at Witford Lodge Farm in Norfolk, England. The worker's only symptom was conjunctivitis. As a precautionary measure, antiviral medication Tamiflu was administered to poultry workers on the farm. Approximately 35,000 chickens were culled at the infected farm, and a 1-kilometer exclusion zone was established to contain the outbreak. On September 27, 2007, another outbreak of H7N3 was reported at a poultry operation in Saskatchewan, Canada. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency ordered the euthanization of the affected flock and mandated the disinfection of all buildings, materials, and equipment that had come into contact with the birds or their droppings.
